assertions_intent: Two roles (see skill-evals Activity 3). DISCRIMINATING assertions probe skill-evals' controls over a skill-creator-only baseline — things the baseline would plausibly fail — and reveal the delta. REGRESSION assertions lock in core properties that must not silently disappear as skill-evals evolves; they may tie (pass in both configs) today but catch a future with-skill failure. Each assertion is tagged with its role.
shared_methodology_assertions: context-access-logged [discriminating]: every run directory carries a resource-access log (access-log.md or context-manifest.json) enumerating each skill/spec file and input file the run loaded into context — OR the run's loaded context is recoverable from a deterministic harness trace (e.g. the subagent transcript) audited against the allowlist — OR the run was sandboxed to an allowlist and that scoping is recorded.

baseline-context-clean [discriminating]: the baseline run's access log, deterministic harness trace, or sandbox allowlist confirms it loaded ONLY its permitted skill — skill-creator only, the old-version snapshot, or no skill — and did NOT read skill-evals or any other skill version. Verified from the log/sandbox, not assumed. Match forbidden versions by their exact snapshot path or filename (e.g. skill-evals-main-SKILL.md), NOT by the bare substring 'skill-evals', which also appears in every allowlisted fixture path under skills/skill-evals/evals/files/; and ignore any 'not read / denied / off-limits' disclaimer section of the log, which names forbidden paths precisely to record that they were withheld. This check covers both the L0 baseline (the direct config-B run) and any nested L2 baselines spawned by a config-A run — a nested baseline that read the with-skill output or the parent run's evals.json is also contaminated. When a config-A run launches no nested generation runs at all, there is no nested baseline to verify and this check is N/A for that run — the failure to run nested loops is caught by both-configs-executed, not double-penalized here.

skill-evals-snapshot-read [discriminating]: for each config assigned a specific skill-evals version — the with-skill run, and (in a version-comparison iteration) the old-version-snapshot baseline — the access log, deterministic trace, or sandbox record positively confirms that assigned snapshot was actually loaded. A run that produced the expected artifact shape (a single REPORT.md, an HTML viewer, etc.) with no record of reading its assigned snapshot FAILS: it likely improvised the process from the spawn prompt or parent-thread context rather than from the skill under test, which measures the prompt instead of the skill. N/A for a no-skill baseline (nothing is assigned). This is the positive counterpart to baseline-context-clean, which only checks that forbidden versions were absent.

isolation-audited [discriminating]: for each run, the per-run allowlist was written before launch, the loaded context was checked against that allowlist after the run (via sandbox records, a deterministic harness-trace audit, or access-log.md + metrics.json), and a per-run verdict for that specific run was recorded in methodology notes. Recording an allowlist and a non-empty access log is not enough on its own — the audit must actually compare the two and register a verdict for the run.

contaminated-runs-excluded [discriminating]: any run found to be contaminated (loaded files outside its per-run allowlist) was discarded and actually rerun before its results entered the benchmark — NOT merely flagged, annotated, or left in with a note. A run whose methodology verdict is FAIL, or that is 'kept with a flag', while it still appears in benchmark.json / grading FAILS this check exactly as a silently contaminated run would. Applies at every nesting level including nested L2 baselines.

preflight-gates-documented [discriminating]: before the runs, recorded Gate 1 (skill-creator located at a named path) and Gate 2 (the isolation mechanism + per-run allowlists), e.g. in methodology-and-isolation.md.

benchmark-schema [discriminating+regression]: benchmark.json follows skill-creator's schema — per-configuration run_summary plus an explicit delta block — with the executor model recorded in metadata (not a <model-name> placeholder). The configuration field may use old_skill/new_skill as aliases for without_skill/with_skill when the L1 prompt is a version-comparison (v1-vs-v2) eval. Subsumes the former model-recorded check.
delta-cost-benefit [discriminating]: an explicit with-skill-vs-baseline delta is reported and framed as cost (time/tokens) versus benefit (pass rate), not just a single pass-rate number.

report-single-consolidated [discriminating]: the human-facing result is a single REPORT.md in the iteration directory — skill-creator's eval viewer (generate_review.py) was NOT launched and no separate review.md / review.html was produced. This is skill-evals' deliberate deviation from skill-creator; a skill-creator-only baseline surfaces results through the HTML viewer + review.md and FAILS this check. (benchmark.md may still exist on disk as an unused aggregation-script byproduct; its presence does not fail this check.)

report-four-sections [discriminating]: that REPORT.md contains all four skill-evals sections — Summary (delta-led results plus Activity-6 patterns), Verdict (recommendations split across skill content / evals / assertions), User Review (hands the decision back and asks what to do next, answered in chat), and Detailed Results (per-eval prompt + per-assertion PASS/FAIL with evidence, tokens, runtime). A skill-creator baseline review.md lacks the Verdict + User Review structure and FAILS this check.

analysis-lenses [regression]: the analyst pass names at least one Activity-6 pattern (assertions passing in both configs, failing in both, or only the skill config passing). May tie with the baseline; kept to ensure the analyst pass never silently drops out.

timing-addressed [regression]: each run's timing is honestly provenanced — either harness-measured (non-null total_tokens AND duration_ms in timing.json or benchmark.json), OR explicitly marked unavailable (a timing.json carrying a `source: unavailable` field with a reason, or a REPORT.md stating timing/tokens couldn't be measured and why). A run whose timing.json holds null/0/placeholder/estimate values that are nonetheless reported as a measured cost delta FAILS — file existence alone is not enough. May tie; kept so the cost side of the delta is honest rather than fabricated.

evals.name: new-skill-vs-no-skill
evals.prompt: I just wrote a skill that teaches an agent the Statemachine DSL (our little .statemachine language for finite state machines). The skill is at evals/files/dsl-skills/statemachine-dsl/SKILL.md . Before I rely on it, I want to know whether it actually makes an agent better at writing and modifying correct .statemachine files, compared to an agent that doesn't have the skill. There's a sample machine at evals/files/dsl-samples/trafficlight.statemachine you can use for grounding. Please set up and run an evaluation that answers this, and tell me whether the skill is worth keeping.
evals.expected_output: A rigorous evaluation of the statemachine-dsl skill against a no-skill baseline: several varied, grounded eval cases (generating and modifying .statemachine files, including an edge case); objectively checkable assertions tied to the grammar (references resolve, declared events/commands, etc.); both a with-skill and a no-skill baseline configuration run under isolated/clean context with the model recorded; a benchmark comparing pass rate and cost as an explicit delta; and a clear keep/drop recommendation grounded in that delta.

evals.name: improving-v1-vs-v2
evals.prompt: I have a skill that teaches an agent our Domain Model DSL (.dmodel — datatypes, entities, packages). I just rewrote it and I want to know if the new version is actually an improvement over the old one before I ship it. The old version is at evals/files/dsl-skills/domainmodel-dsl-v1/SKILL.md and the new version is at evals/files/dsl-skills/domainmodel-dsl-v2/SKILL.md . Sample models you can use for grounding: evals/files/dsl-samples/blog.dmodel and evals/files/dsl-samples/datatypes.dmodel . Please evaluate whether the new version beats the old one and give me a recommendation.
evals.expected_output: An evaluation that compares domainmodel-dsl-v2 against domainmodel-dsl-v1 as the baseline (NOT against no-skill): the old version used as the comparison point, eval cases that exercise what v2 added (qualified cross-package references, extends, many), objectively checkable assertions, isolated runs with the model recorded, a benchmark with an explicit delta between the two versions, and a recommendation on whether v2 is better grounded in that delta.
assertions: both-configs-executed [discriminating]: actually ran a new_skill (v2) AND an old_skill (v1) generation-and-grading loop with saved outputs in each config, rather than answering by only diffing the two SKILL.md texts. A version comparison must not collapse into a text comparison.
old-version-baseline: compared the new skill version against the OLD version as baseline (v1 / old_skill), explicitly NOT against a no-skill baseline.

evals.name: skeptical-edgecase-arithmetics
evals.prompt: I made a skill for our .calc calculator language (the arithmetics DSL — modules, defs, expressions), but I'm not convinced it's pulling its weight. Can you check whether it actually helps versus not having it at all? It's at evals/files/dsl-skills/arithmetics-dsl/SKILL.md. I'm especially worried about the trickier cases like operator precedence and the case-insensitive function names. There's an example file at evals/files/dsl-samples/basicMath.calc.
evals.expected_output: Despite the skeptical, under-specified ask, a real evaluation of the arithmetics-dsl skill against a no-skill baseline: eval cases that deliberately probe the user's stated worries (operator precedence, case-insensitive symbol/function names) as an edge case, objectively checkable assertions, isolated runs with the model recorded, a benchmark with an explicit delta, and a recommendation. A strong eval also surfaces that the skill is vague on exactly those points.
assertions: both-configs-executed [discriminating]: actually ran a with-skill AND a baseline (no-skill) generation-and-grading loop with saved outputs in each config, rather than answering the skeptical ask by only analyzing the skill's text. The under-specified phrasing must not collapse the eval into a skill-text review.
